An 8-ball pool game in which two AI agents compete on one shared table, with every search algorithm from the course used inside the game.

Abstract

CueMind is a two-player pool game built for the Artificial Intelligence laboratory. Instead of standard 8-ball rules it uses a Rack Attack format: both players share one table, each owns a 60-second chess clock that runs only while that player thinks and aims, every potted ball is worth one point and the 8-ball three. The two main players are a Minimax agent (alpha-beta pruning, chance nodes for shot noise and iterative deepening) and a Monte Carlo Tree Search agent (UCB1). The remaining course algorithms do the supporting work: A* plans the run-out order, Greedy best-first is the easy AI and orders moves, BFS places the cue ball after a foul, depth-limited DFS finds bank shots, IDDFS finds kick shots and controls thinking time, and bidirectional search finds combination shots.

The game is written in Python with Pygame. A numba-compiled fixed-step physics engine is shared by the renderer and by the agents, so the shots an agent simulates behave exactly like the shots on screen apart from random execution error. The game offers AI vs AI, Human vs AI and a benchmark mode. This report describes the rules and mechanics, explains each algorithm with pseudocode, traces one decision through every algorithm step by step, and reports the results of 40 benchmark matches, in which both search agents beat the greedy baseline and MCTS edged Minimax 11–9.

1Introduction and objectives

Board games such as tic-tac-toe are the usual setting for adversarial search, but their moves are discrete and their outcomes are certain. Pool is harder: a shot is a continuous choice of angle and power, the result depends on physics, and even a perfect plan can miss. The project brief required a game in which at least two AI agents play against each other. We chose pool to show how classic search algorithms can be adapted to a continuous, stochastic game.

  • Build a complete, playable pool game with an AI vs AI mode and a Human vs AI mode.
  • Implement Minimax and MCTS as competing players and compare them fairly.
  • Give every other algorithm from the course (A*, Greedy, BFS, DFS/DLS, IDDFS, bidirectional search) a real job in the game.
  • Make the decision process visible during play and traceable for analysis.

2Game overview and rules

CueMind uses the Rack Attack Duel format. Two players share one table and alternate turns. Because the table is shared, every shot changes the position the opponent faces, so the agents genuinely play against each other rather than racing on separate tables.

RuleDetail
ClockEach player has 60 s. The clock runs only while that player thinks and aims; it is paused while balls roll.
ScoringAny object ball = 1 point; the 8-ball = 3 points. There are no solids/stripes groups.
TurnPot at least one ball without a foul and you shoot again; otherwise the turn passes.
FoulCue ball pocketed (scratch) or cue ball touches no ball: −1 point, −5 s, and the opponent gets ball-in-hand.
EndThe table is clear or both clocks reach zero. Higher score wins; a tie goes to the player with more clock left.
Break15 balls in a triangle, the 8-ball in the centre; the cue ball starts on the head spot.

The match screen shows two player cards (avatar, score, clock ring and potted balls), a rack tracker and two-sided time bar in the centre, the table, and the AI Vision panel on the right. While an agent thinks, the panel shows its live search statistics, its top five shots and the A* run-out plan; faint lines on the table show the shots being weighed.

3Game mechanics and physics

The table field is 1000 × 500 units with ball radius r = 11.5, six pockets (capture radius 26 for corners, 23 for side pockets) and cushions modelled as line segments, including the angled pocket jaws. One fixed-step engine is used both to animate the game and inside the agents' searches, so a simulated shot reproduces the real shot exactly when the same angle and power are used.

Physics step (dt = 1/240 s)

# one tiny time step (dt = 1/240 second)
for ball in moving_balls:
    ball.position = ball.position + ball.speed * dt      # move a little
    ball.speed = ball.speed - friction * dt            # friction slows it down

for a, b in pairs_of_balls:
    if distance(a, b) < 2 * radius:                     # two balls touch
        swap_speed_along_line(a, b)                     # equal balls trade speed

for ball in balls:
    if ball touches a cushion:   bounce it back (keeps 78% of its speed)
    if ball is near a pocket:    ball.potted = True

The kernels are compiled with numba, so one full shot from strike to rest takes about 3 ms. This lets an agent test several hundred shots per second while it thinks. Agents always simulate on copies of the table and never touch the live game state.

Execution noise

Every AI shot is played with random error: angle error with σ = 0.30° and power error with σ = 2.5%. Both agents get the same noise, which makes pool a stochastic game and is the reason both agents average over several noisy samples of a shot.

Aiming with the ghost ball

Ghost = B − 2r · (P − B) / |P − B|

To send target ball B towards pocket P, the cue ball must arrive at the ghost point, one ball diameter behind B on the line from P through B. The aim angle is the direction from the cue ball to the ghost. A shot is rejected if another ball blocks either the cue path or the object-ball path, if the cut angle exceeds 80°, or if it approaches a side pocket too flatly.

Heuristic: chance that a pot works

σ = d₁·σθ / (2r·cos cut)    α = atan(w / d₂)    p = erf(α / (σ√2)) · (1 − ¼(cut/85°)⁴)    h = p × points

An aiming error of σθ moves the contact point sideways by d₁·σθ, which turns the object ball by about σ. The pot works while that turn stays inside the pocket's angular window α. Here d₁ is the cue-to-ghost distance, d₂ the ball-to-pocket distance and w the usable pocket half-width (62% of the capture radius, narrower for side pockets hit at an angle). The required power is computed from the friction model so the object ball still rolls at about 100 units/s at the pocket; each pot is offered at 1.0×, 1.3× and 1.75× of that power (soft, medium, firm).

4System design

1 · Physicsnumba fixed-step engine; balls, cushions, pockets
2 · Shot finderdirect, bank (DLS), kick (IDDFS), combo (bidirectional), safety
3 · AgentGreedy, Minimax or MCTS chooses a shot within its time budget
4 · Rulespoints, fouls, clocks, turn order, ball-in-hand (BFS)
5 · Renderer3D balls, cue, effects, sound, AI Vision panel

Each turn flows through these five parts. The agent runs in a background thread and searches on a snapshot of the match; meanwhile the main thread keeps animating at 60 fps and drains the player's clock in real time. The thinking budget per shot is 14% of the time left, between 0.25 s and 2.5 s, so agents speed up as their clock runs down. When the agent returns, the cue animates to the chosen angle, the shot is played with execution noise, and the rules module scores the result.

ModuleResponsibility
game/physics.pyTable state, fixed-step simulation, events for sound and effects
game/shots.pyGhost ball, pot chance, direct/bank/kick/combo/safety shots, BFS placement
game/planner.pyA* run-out planner
game/rules.pyRack Attack scoring, fouls, clocks, snapshots for search
game/agents/Greedy, Minimax and MCTS agents; shared evaluation and noisy play
game/render/, game/scenes/Ball shader, table art, cue, particles, synthesized sound, UI; menu, setup, match, results, benchmark, how-to

Evaluation function (used by Minimax leaves and MCTS rewards)

E(s) = (scoreme − scoreopp) ± 0.9 · Q(s) + 0.025 · (clockme − clockopp)

Q(s) is the best heuristic pot value available to whoever moves next; it is added when it is our turn and subtracted when it is the opponent's. Finished matches score the point difference plus ±4 for a win or loss. Values are clamped to [−20, 20], which the chance-node pruning needs. MCTS turns E into a reward in [0, 1] with 1 / (1 + e−E/2).

5.1 Minimax with alpha-beta and chance nodes

Minimax imagines the game as a tree. On MAX levels it is our turn and we pick the shot with the highest value; on MIN levels it is the opponent's turn and we assume they pick the shot that is worst for us. In pool a player who pots shoots again, so two MAX levels can follow each other. Because a real shot can miss, every shot is played a few times with a small random error and the results are averaged. Alpha-beta remembers the best value found so far (α for us, β for the opponent) and stops looking at a branch as soon as it is clear that branch cannot be better. Iterative deepening searches 1 shot ahead, then 2, then 3, so there is always an answer when the clock runs out.

def minimax(state, depth, my_turn, alpha, beta):
    if depth == 0 or game_over(state):
        return evaluate(state)                  # score of this table

    if my_turn:                                 # MAX: I want the highest value
        best = -infinity
        for shot in good_shots(state):
            value = average_of_2_tries(state, shot, depth)   # shots can miss
            best = max(best, value)
            alpha = max(alpha, best)
            if alpha >= beta:
                break                           # alpha-beta: skip the rest
        return best
    else:                                       # MIN: opponent wants the lowest
        best = +infinity
        for shot in good_shots(state):
            value = average_of_2_tries(state, shot, depth)
            best = min(best, value)
            beta = min(beta, best)
            if alpha >= beta:
                break
        return best

# iterative deepening: try depth 1, then 2, then 3 ... until time is up
for depth in [1, 2, 3, 4]:
    if time_is_up(): break
    best_shot = the shot with the best minimax value at this depth

5.2 Monte Carlo Tree Search (UCB1)

UCB1(child) = W/N + C·√(ln Nparent / N),   C = 1.4

for i in range(many_times):                         # until the time is up
    node = root
    # 1. Selection: go down the tree using UCB1
    while node is fully expanded:
        node = child with the highest  Q + C * sqrt(ln(N_parent) / N)
    # 2. Expansion: add one new shot we have not tried
    node = node.add_new_child()
    # 3. Simulation: play the shot (with a little random error) and one more quick shot
    reward = play_out_and_score(node)            # number between 0 and 1
    # 4. Backpropagation: tell every node on the path how it went
    while node is not None:
        node.N = node.N + 1
        node.W = node.W + reward
        node = node.parent

best_shot = root child with the most visits

Below the root an action means "the k-th best shot in the position reached" (k = 1..4), because the actual shots depend on where the balls stop after each noisy simulation.

5.3 A* run-out planner

A state is the cue-ball position plus the set of balls still to pot. Potting ball b in pocket q costs −ln p + 0.15, combining difficulty with a fixed time cost per shot; the cue ball is assumed to stop near the ghost point. Every remaining ball needs at least one shot costing at least 0.15, so h = (balls left) × 0.15 never overestimates: it is admissible and A* returns the cheapest order it finds. To stay fast it plans the five balls nearest the cue ball with at most 2500 expansions.

open_list = [ (f=0, cue_position, balls_left, plan=[]) ]
while open_list:
    node = take the node with the smallest f      # f = g + h
    if no balls left in node:
        return node.plan                          # cheapest order found
    for ball in node.balls_left:
        cost = -log(pot_chance(ball)) + 0.15      # hard shot = high cost
        g = node.g + cost                         # cost so far
        h = (number of balls left - 1) * 0.15     # guess of cost still to pay
        add (g + h, new cue position, balls_left - ball, plan + [ball]) to open_list

5.4 Greedy best-first (Easy AI)

best_score = -1
for shot in direct_pots:
    score = pot_chance(shot) * points(shot)     # h = p x points
    if score > best_score:
        best_score = score
        best_shot = shot
play(best_shot)                                 # no thinking about the future

5.5 BFS: ball-in-hand placement

queue = [ideal_spot]
visited = {ideal_spot}
while queue:
    spot = queue.pop(0)                         # first in, first out
    if spot is inside the table and touches no ball:
        return spot                             # nearest free spot
    for next_spot in the 8 neighbours of spot:
        if next_spot not in visited:
            visited.add(next_spot)
            queue.append(next_spot)

Because each grid step costs the same, the first legal cell found is the one nearest to the ideal spot. The agents run BFS from the four best ideal spots and keep the placement with the best next pot.

5.6 DFS / depth-limited search: bank shots

def find_bank(path_of_cushions, limit):
    if len(path_of_cushions) == limit:
        if the ball can travel this cushion path into the pocket:
            save this bank shot
        return
    for cushion in ["top", "bottom", "left", "right"]:
        find_bank(path_of_cushions + [cushion], limit)      # go one level deeper

find_bank([], limit=1)       # banks off 1 cushion
find_bank([], limit=2)       # banks off 2 cushions

The mirror image is scaled by the cushion restitution (y' = c − (y − c)/e) so the predicted rebound angle matches the engine. Bank shots use limits 1 and 2.

5.7 IDDFS: kick shots

for limit in [0, 1, 2, 3]:              # 0 cushions = straight line
    shots = find_kick(cue_ball, limit)  # depth-limited search (as above)
    if shots:
        return shots                    # stop at the fewest cushions

Kicks are generated only when no pot or safety exists (the cue ball is snookered), so the simplest legal escape is found first. The same deepen-until-time-runs-out idea is used by Minimax (Section 5.1).

5.8 Bidirectional search: combination shots

# search 1 (forward): balls the cue ball can hit directly
forward = [ball for ball in balls if line_is_clear(cue_ball, ball)]

# search 2 (backward): balls that can drop into a pocket
backward = [ball for ball in balls if line_is_clear(ball, pocket)]

# where the two searches meet = a combination shot
for A in forward:
    for B in backward:
        if A != B and line_is_clear(A, B):
            save combo shot: cue ball -> A -> B -> pocket

Searching from both ends only pairs balls that are already reachable from the cue and already pottable, instead of trying every cue → A → B → pocket chain.

6Step-by-step decision analysis

To show how decisions are made, one fixed position was traced through every algorithm with logging enabled. The rack (seed 11) was broken with a fixed shot; no ball dropped and Minimax is to move with all 15 balls on the table, both scores 0 and both clocks at 60 s. For readable trees the trace uses smaller widths than the live game: Minimax root width 4, inner width 3, two samples per root shot and one inside; MCTS uses 160 iterations over the top 8 shots.

Step 1: candidate shots and their heuristic

The shot finder produced 16 direct pots, 11 bank shots (DLS), 1 combination (bidirectional) and 22 safeties. Table 1 shows the four best direct pots.

Worked example, shot A. σ = 50.5 × 0.30° / (2 × 11.5 × cos 33.9°) = 15.15 / 19.09 = 0.79°. α = atan(w / 145.6) = 4.91°. p = erf(4.91 / (0.79 × √2)) × (1 − ¼(33.9/85)⁴) = 1.000 × 0.994 = 0.994, so h = 0.994 × 1 point. Shot C pots the same ball but its long d₂ shrinks the pocket window α to 1.58°, and shot D is almost straight but its long d₁ makes σ large. Greedy stops here and plays shot A.

A* considered the five balls nearest the cue ball (2, 4, 7, 8, 9) and returned the order 2 → bottom side, 4 → bottom-right, 9 → bottom-right, 7 → top side, 8 → top-right, with total cost 2.28 after 24 expansions. For example, step 2 expands "pot 2 into the bottom side": g = −ln 0.994 + 0.15 = 0.156 and four balls remain, so h = 4 × 0.15 = 0.60. The first planned pot receives a small ordering bonus in Minimax and MCTS, which encourages them to try position-friendly shots first.

Step 3: Minimax with iterative deepening

Root shotDepth 1 valueDepth 2 value
2 → bottom side, soft+1.632+1.528
2 → bottom side, medium+1.548+2.789
2 → bottom side, firm+1.514+2.674
9 → bottom-right, soft+0.500−0.500

Depth 1 (8 simulations, 21 nodes) evaluates the position right after each shot and prefers the soft pot (+1.63). Depth 2 (30 simulations, 87 nodes, 2 branches pruned) also searches the next shot. After the medium-power pot the cue ball stops where ball 15 can be potted into the top-right pocket, so medium now scores +2.79 and Minimax changes its decision. If time ran out during depth 3, it would still play this depth-2 choice. This is the advantage of iterative deepening.

Inside the winning branch

Both noisy samples potted ball 2 (score 1–0), so Minimax shoots again and the child is a MAX node. Each MAX node tries three follow-ups on ball 15. In sample 1 the firm follow-up is best (+2.90); in sample 2 the soft one is (+2.68). The chance node averages them: (2.90 + 2.68) / 2 = +2.79.

Alpha-beta cut in this trace. When "9 → bottom-right, soft" was searched, α was already +2.79. The shot missed, so the opponent moved (MIN node). The opponent's first reply already gave a value below α, so the MIN node could never return more than α and its remaining two replies were skipped. Pruning saved work without changing the result, as alpha-beta guarantees. The Star1 rule applies the same idea across the noisy samples of a chance node.

Step 4: Monte Carlo Tree Search

UCB1 worked example for the most-visited child "2 → bottom side, soft": N = 23, W = 14.96, so Q = 14.96 / 23 = 0.651. The exploration term is 1.4 × √(ln 160 / 23) = 1.4 × √(5.075 / 23) = 0.658, so UCB1 = 0.651 + 0.658 = 1.308. A less-visited child such as "2 → bottom-left, soft" (N = 16, Q = 0.505) gets a larger exploration term (0.788), so its UCB1 (1.293) stays close. All children end near 1.30, which is UCB1 balancing exploration and exploitation.
IterRoot shot selectedRewardNQ
12 → bottom side, soft0.78810.788

Progressive widening opens new root children slowly: one child at first, more as visits grow (⌈1.5·√(N+1)⌉). The first iterations therefore alternate between expanding new shots in heuristic order and revisiting the best ones. Each iteration replays the selected shots with fresh noise, adds one greedy play-out shot and backs up a reward between 0 and 1. After 160 iterations the root's most-visited child is 2 → bottom side, soft (23 visits, Q = 0.65), which MCTS plays.

Step 5: comparing the three decisions

AgentDecisionReason
Greedy2 → bottom side, softHighest single-shot heuristic (0.994); no look-ahead
Minimax2 → bottom side, mediumDepth 2 sees the follow-up pot on ball 15; value +2.79 vs +1.53 for soft
MCTS2 → bottom side, softMost visits (23 of 160) after noisy play-outs; Q = 0.65

All three agents choose to pot ball 2 into the bottom side pocket, which confirms that the heuristic ranks pots sensibly. They differ on power. Minimax's exhaustive depth-2 search plans the cue-ball position for the next shot. MCTS, with one play-out shot and noisy estimates, found that the extra power did not clearly pay off within 160 iterations. This trade-off between systematic look-ahead and sampled estimates is exactly what the benchmark measures.

7Results and evaluation

Benchmark mode plays silent matches with identical physics and execution noise for both sides; each agent gets 0.6 s of thinking per shot, charged to its clock, and the breaker alternates each game. We ran 40 matches.

Matchup (A vs B)MatchesWins AWins BAvg score AAvg score BFouls / match AFouls / match B
Minimax vs MCTS209117.559.150.200.10
Greedy vs Minimax10195.1011.600.100.20
Greedy vs MCTS10377.609.200.200.00
  • Both search agents clearly beat the greedy baseline (9–1 and 7–3), so looking ahead pays off even under shot noise.
  • MCTS edged Minimax 11–9 with a higher average score (9.15 vs 7.55). Twenty matches are too few to call this difference significant; the two are close at this time budget.
  • Fouls are rare for every agent (at most 0.2 per match), because both the search and the evaluation penalize scratches.

8Conclusion and future work

CueMind shows that classic search algorithms adapt well to a continuous, stochastic game once the game is reduced to a small set of meaningful moves. The ghost-ball shot finder, built from DLS, IDDFS and bidirectional search, turns infinite angles into a few dozen candidates. A* and Greedy rank them, and Minimax (with chance nodes, Star1 pruning and IDDFS) and MCTS (with UCB1) decide under a real time limit. Both agents are fully functional and beat the greedy baseline. The step-by-step trace shows Minimax changing its decision as it searches deeper, and MCTS converging through UCB1.

Future work: add spin (top/back/side) to give position play more control; parallelize MCTS play-outs across CPU cores; learn the evaluation weights from benchmark data; and run larger benchmarks with confidence intervals for each time budget.
